name: Wrist and forearm stretch
pattern: Static hold: the wrist bends back or forward with the elbow straight, lengthening the forearm flexors or extensors.
setup: Stand or sit tall, shoulders down.
Reach one arm straight forward at shoulder height, palm up.
Other hand holds the fingers of the reaching hand.

steps.text: Straighten the elbow fully, then gently pull the fingers down and back.
Stay still 15-30 s. Feel it along the inside of the forearm. Turn the palm down and bend the wrist for the outside.
Come out slowly, then switch sides.

cues.why: The forearm muscles cross the elbow; bending it slackens them.

cues.cue: Pull slowly with the other hand, no yanking.
cues.why: Slow, steady holds of 30-45 s are what tendon programs use.
Shrugging adds neck tension and does not help the stretch.

cues.cue: Ease in to a mild pull, never pain.
cues.why: Gentle stretches still gain range; stretching into pain did not help and can irritate the muscle.

cues.cue: Hold 15-30 s, 2-4 times, about 60 s in total per side.
cues.why: 30 s holds gave the same gains as 60 s; aim for at least 5 min per muscle each week, most days.

breathing: Breathe slowly and normally. Ease a little deeper as you breathe out.

tempo.note: Ease in for about 3 s, hold 15-30 s, ease out. Repeat 2-4 times each side.

mistakes.name: Elbow bent
mistakes.looks: The reaching arm bends as you pull on the fingers.
mistakes.fix: Lock the elbow out softly first, then pull less hard.
mistakes.why: The stretch on the forearm muscles is lost.

mistakes.name: Pulling too hard
mistakes.looks: You crank the hand back fast to the end of range.
mistakes.fix: Ease in to a mild pull and hold.
mistakes.why: Wrist ligaments and tendons are small and irritate easily.

mistakes.name: Holding your breath
mistakes.looks: You tense up: shoulders creep up, jaw tight, breath held.
mistakes.fix: Breathe slowly; let each breath out take you a little deeper.
mistakes.why: Tension fights the stretch; relaxed breathing lets the muscle let go.

safety: Tingling or numbness in the fingers: ease off, a nerve is being pulled.
Tennis or golfer's elbow: keep it mild; pain should not linger after.

variants.change: Hands on the floor or a wall, fingers pointing back: body weight gives the stretch, lean only a little.
Fingers or thumb pulled back one at a time: smaller, more local stretch.
Contract-relax: push gently against the stretch for 3-6 s, relax, then ease deeper. Similar range gains to static holds; also best after training.
A partner moves the limb. Go slowly and say when you feel a mild pull; the partner holds there, never pushes into pain.
Moving version: controlled swings through the range, 8-12 reps. Better before training than long holds.

subtypes.name: Kneeling wrist stretch
subtypes.change: On hands and knees, turn the hands so the fingers point to your knees; lean back slowly.

subtypes.name: Wrist extensor stretch
subtypes.change: Arm forward, palm down; bend the wrist so the fingers point down and press gently on the back of the hand.

subtypes.name: Finger and thumb stretch
subtypes.change: Pull one finger or the thumb gently back, or spread the fingers wide; elbow straight.

subtypes.name: Forearm rotation stretch
subtypes.change: Elbow straight or bent at your side; turn the palm fully up or down and help gently with the other hand.

metrics.label: Movement during hold
metrics.good: < 3° once you are in the stretch

motion.basis: Hold time from stasinopoulos2005 and garber2011. Wrist ranges are estimates from typical end range (about 70° each way); finger and deviation positions have no joint key, so wristExt and forearm stand in. Little direct research on these stretches.
